summary: Presents a framework for recovery in MPLS networks. To deliver reliable service, label switching routers need procedures for fault detection, fault notification and fault recovery, and signaling must support configuring recovery. It describes the concepts and terminology for protecting traffic on different paths.

eli5.summary: If a road gets blocked, traffic should switch to a spare route quickly. This note describes the general plan for noticing problems and switching paths in MPLS networks.

subtitle: The vocabulary, principles and comparison criteria for protecting MPLS traffic when links or nodes fail.

tldr.problem: IP routing can take several seconds (IGPs) or minutes (BGP) to recover from a fault, which is too slow for services that need recovery in seconds down to tens of milliseconds.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines two recovery models, rerouting and protection switching, with shared terminology, recovery cycle timing, options for scope and resources, and criteria for comparing schemes.
tldr.outcome: It is a conceptual Informational framework, not a protocol. The authors expected a standards track document to follow, and RFC 5462 has since updated this one.

facts.label: Target recovery time
facts.value: Seconds down to tens of milliseconds

today: RFC 3469 is an Informational RFC that has been updated by RFC 5462; it has not been obsoleted. It is a framework of concepts and terminology rather than a protocol specification.

sections.title: Why MPLS Needs Its Own Recovery
sections.content:
Routing algorithms are robust, but the time they take to recover from a fault can be several seconds for interior gateway protocols and minutes for BGP. That is unacceptable where recovery should take seconds down to tens of milliseconds, for example for Virtual Leased Line services, voice and video. IP routing also cannot easily give bandwidth recovery, meaning an alternative path with equivalent bandwidth.

The RFC argues that MPLS-based recovery is faster than Layer 3 rerouting while keeping Layer 3 visibility. It can protect specific flows, be less wasteful than Layer 0 or Layer 1 mechanisms such as SONET, and avoids the coarse granularity of lower layers. An LSP is source routed, so a recovery path can be pinned and is not disturbed by transient instability in SPF routing.

The goals include meeting traffic engineering aims, restoration times that fit the application (as short as tens of milliseconds in some cases), no single points of failure, minimal packet loss and reordering, and minimal state and signaling overhead. The authors note that some goals conflict and call for trade-offs. They also state that the framework is conceptual, and that parts are the authors' opinions rather than the consolidated views of the IETF.
sections.eli5: Normal internet repair is like waiting for a whole town to learn about a closed road. MPLS can have a detour ready so traffic switches almost at once.

sections.title: Recovery Models and Terminology
sections.content:
There are two basic models. Rerouting establishes new paths on demand after a fault, using signaling. Protection switching pre-establishes a recovery path, and when a fault is detected the protected traffic is switched onto it. The two can be combined: switch to a recovery path for speed, then reroute later for a better configuration.

The key roles are the working path (carries traffic before a fault), the recovery path (carries it after), the Path Switch LSR (PSL), which switches or replicates traffic between them, and the Path Merge LSR (PML), which receives recovery traffic and merges it back or delivers it. The Point of Repair (POR) is the LSR that performs the repair, and may be a PSL or PML.

Other defined terms include revertive and non-revertive mode, bypass tunnel, path group, protected path group and protected traffic portion. Faults are classed as Path Failure, Path Degraded, Link Failure and Link Degraded. A Fault Indication Signal (FIS) travels to the POR, and a Fault Recovery Signal (FRS) reports a repair.
sections.eli5: Rerouting is drawing a detour after the road closes. Protection switching is having the detour already marked on the map. One worker flips the traffic to the detour, and another worker lets it back onto the road.

sections.title: The Recovery Cycles
sections.content:
The framework models time. In the recovery cycle, five intervals run from the network impairment to traffic being recovered: T1 fault detection, T2 fault hold-off, T3 fault notification, T4 recovery operation and T5 traffic recovery. The hold-off time is a configured wait that lets lower layer protection act first, and it may be zero.

In the reversion cycle (revertive protection switching), traffic goes back to the preferred path once the fault clears. Its intervals are T7 to T11, and T6 is the time the impairment stays unrepaired. A clear hold-off time helps avoid flapping when a fault is intermittent. The RFC prefers a well-controlled switch-back with minimal disruption over an immediate one.

In the dynamic re-routing cycle (T12 to T15), routing protocols converge and traffic moves to a possibly new working path. The RFC gives an example: a link fails, a FIS reaches the PSL, the PSL switches to the pre-configured recovery path, routing converges, a new working path is set up between the PSL and PML, and traffic moves to it.
sections.eli5: Fixing a road takes steps: notice the problem, tell the traffic controller, wait a moment in case the road fixes itself, then move the cars. The note gives a name and a timer to each step.

sections.title: Principles of MPLS-Based Recovery
sections.content:
Fastest recovery is assumed to come from protection switching, with LSR switch completion comparable to the 50 ms switch-over of the SONET layer. Recovery can be enabled per path: either default recovery (only IP rerouting or a lower layer) or recoverable. Paths can be set up with RSVP-TE, CR-LDP or other means including SNMP, and may be pre-established, pre-qualified or established-on-demand. Resources may be pre-reserved or reserved-on-demand. A recovery path that can replace the working path without degrading service is equivalent, otherwise it is limited.

In 1+1 protection the recovery path carries a copy of the traffic and the PML selects between the two. In 1:1 protection the recovery path may carry preemptible low priority traffic until it is needed. This extends to 1:n and m:n.

Scope options include local repair (the node upstream of the fault acts, protecting a link or neighbor node), global repair (a distant POR is told by a FIS), alternate egress repair, multi-layer repair and concatenated protection domains. Path mapping can be 1-to-1, n-to-1, n-to-m or split path, and a bypass tunnel can back up a group of paths using label stacking. Protection can cover part of the traffic on a path or a bundle of paths.
sections.eli5: You can keep a spare road empty and ready, or let other cars use it until there is an emergency. A spare road can also help many main roads at once.

sections.title: Detecting and Signaling Faults
sections.content:
MPLS recovery starts after a lower layer fault, an IP layer fault or a fault in MPLS mechanisms. Path failure can be found with a path continuity test or a periodic liveness message between neighbor LSRs, and a probe must follow the same route as the path it tests. Path degraded is a quality problem such as excessive packet discarding, and counts as a fault only when lost packets exceed a provisioned threshold. Lower layers can report link failure or degradation, such as SONET loss of signal, sometimes faster than MPLS can detect it.

A node that cannot repair the fault itself sends a FIS to the POR, by control plane messaging hop by hop or by user plane messaging toward the PML. Because the FIS is a control message it should be sent with high priority.

Triggers may be automatic or external operator commands. After recovery, fixed (pinned) protection counterparts run in revertive or non-revertive mode, while dynamic counterparts are re-established after routing converges. In revertive mode, make-before-break switching minimizes packet loss and reordering.
sections.eli5: Neighbors keep saying I am still here to each other. When one goes quiet, the nearest neighbor sends an urgent message to the worker who can switch the traffic.

sections.title: Comparing Recovery Schemes
sections.content:
The RFC offers criteria for judging schemes. Recovery time is the sum of fault detection, hold-off, notification, recovery operation and traffic restoration times. Others are full restoration time, setup vulnerability (how long paths are left unprotected), backup capacity, additive latency, quality of protection, re-ordering, state overhead, packet loss and coverage.

Coverage covers fault types, concurrent faults, number of recovery paths, percentage of faults covered, and the ratio of protection n/N, where n is the number of protected paths and N the total.

Recovery paths are described by a resource class (equivalent or limited, with lower and best effort classes), a priority attribute and a preemption attribute. Desired features include identifying protected path groups and traffic portions, allowing manual switching commands, and handling merged path segments properly.

On security, the RFC says the recovery it describes raises no issues beyond those already in the MPLS architecture, and that confidentiality on the recovery path is out of scope.
sections.eli5: To pick the best detour plan, you score it on how fast it works, how much spare road it needs, how many cars get lost, and how many kinds of road closures it can handle.

items.label: Fault Detection Time
items.desc: From the network impairment until MPLS-based recovery detects the fault.

items.label: Fault Hold-off Time
items.desc: Configured wait so lower layer protection can act first; may be zero.

items.label: Fault Notification Time
items.desc: From the FIS being sent until the PSL begins recovery.

items.label: Recovery Operation Time
items.desc: Between the first and last recovery actions.

items.label: Traffic Recovery Time
items.desc: Until traffic is completely recovered at the PML.
